evidence_notes: Claim: studying Venus is a worthy pursuit despite its dangers. Support: two marked quotations from 'The Challenge of Exploring Venus' (800 degrees F / 90x atmospheric pressure; gear-and-lever computers needing no electronics), each followed by a one-sentence gloss. org 4 (thesis stated first sentence and held, opening and conventional closing present, both body parts relate, but the Earth-features and old-technology parts swap freely - rung 5 NO); dev 4 (quoted figures are specific and the connection is stated - 'This explain that its too dangers...', 'This quite says that...' - but the gloss restates the quote rather than adding, so rung 5 NO); conv 3 (misspellings accumulate throughout - prusuit, depite, electronies, fromt he pass - and 'it might almost- like features of Earth' and 'This quite says' need re-reading to repair, but nothing has to be guessed - rung 4 NO); arg 3 (position clear and held through the closing - rung 3 YES - but no reason is reasoned: the essay never says why Earth-like features or usable old technology make the pursuit worth the danger, and the second body part ends by undercutting itself - rung 4 NO).

Claim: FACS is not valuable in a classroom because students, especially teens, hide emotions deliberately. Support: Ekman's six named emotions plus a realized hypothetical (reacting to someone who smells, FACS broadcasting the disgust); Dr. Huang's quotation on nonverbal communication, answered by the writer. org 3 (controlling idea stated first sentence, but the third part starts on Huang's quote and finishes on 'Technology is simply taking over the world and people minds set' - a digression that leaves the classroom question, and unity breaks there - rung 4 NO); dev 4 (the smell scenario is specific and its connection is stated - 'That would not only hurt the other person's feelings but make you feel mean' - rung 4 YES; but the teens-hide-emotions premise is general, so support is not specific throughout - rung 5 NO); conv 3 (spacing before punctuation, 'they'er', 'if you was talking', an unclosed quotation in para 3, and 'sit not and talk' force re-reading; meaning stays recoverable - rung 4 NO); arg 4 (why is on the page: exposure invites questioning about a student's private life, so a device that displays feelings harms them - rung 4 YES; Huang is quoted and rejected, but by bare assertion, and the conclusion is the one the prompt's framing already implies - rung 5 NO).

Claim: autonomous cars should be implemented in everyday life because transportation becomes easier and cheaper. Support: Google testing since 2009 and its safety work; an assertion of better fuel economy leading to affordability; a closing taxi-service point. org 4 (thesis at end of para 1 and held, opening orients, closing present, single body part relates - rung 4 YES; the safety and cost units inside it swap freely - rung 5 NO); dev 3 (only 'tested and worked on since 2009 / Google' is specific; fuel economy, affordability and 'easier on the whole of humanity' are general gestures the reader must connect, and no figure or case is given - rung 4 NO); conv 3 (thay, pasangers, infustructure, econmomy, soceity accumulate, and 'they would for more fuel econmomy' and 'In, conclusion' need repair on re-reading; meaning recoverable - rung 4 NO); arg 4 (one reason is reasoned - better fuel economy makes the transportation system more affordable, extended in the close to cars as a taxi service costing owners nothing to maintain - rung 4 YES; no opposing view, no qualification, no explicit principle - rung 5 NO).

Claim: self-driving cars should be accepted rather than held off. Support: 70+ years of development as a reason not to abandon the work; a realized hypothetical of a person unable to drive whose 'dreams can come true'; a safety paragraph that is pure assertion. org 4 (controlling idea in para 1 and held, opening orients, closing present, all three parts relate - rung 4 YES; the persistence, disability and safety parts are interchangeable - rung 5 NO); dev 3 (the disabled-driver example is specific and explained, but the persistence paragraph offers only a rhetorical question and the safety paragraph offers no support at all - at least one specific, most general - rung 4 fails to hold across the essay); conv 4 (vehical, thier, intellegent, worlds recur, but sentence shapes genuinely vary - rhetorical question, imperative, longer conditional - and nothing needs repair - rung 4 YES; repeated misspellings are more than occasional - rung 5 NO); arg 4 (why is stated: cars that drive themselves let people who cannot drive ride and 'drive' - rung 4 YES; the safety objection is raised but deferred rather than answered - 'as soon as companies make sure these vehicals are 100% safe' - and the conclusion stays inside the prompt's framing - rung 5 NO).

Claim: the Electoral College should be abolished because it is unfair and prone to breakdown. Support: cited quotations from Plumer (electors uncontrollable, winner-take-all producing swing-state-only campaigns, two slates of electors, 'a few swing voters away from catastrophe') and, in a concession paragraph, two from Posner. org 4 (thesis in the first sentence, restated in the close, all parts on the controlling idea, frame present - rung 4 YES; the unfairness and failure-risk parts swap without loss once the 'not only... also' signals are discounted - rung 5 NO); dev 4 (support is specific and cited throughout and the connection is stated after each quote, but most glosses restate the quotation - electors 'might not even vote for who the people want', states 'left out of the campaign' - only the two-slates passage adds an inference - rung 5 NO); conv 4 (disater, campagins, destory recur and the concession paragraph reads awkwardly, but sentences stay under control and vary, and nothing needs repair - rung 4 YES; errors are more than occasional - rung 5 NO); arg 4 (reasons are reasoned - winner-take-all gives candidates no incentive to campaign in safe states, so those voters are ignored - rung 4 YES; the opposing side is presented at length but never answered, the essay simply drops it and re-asserts the thesis - rung 5 NO).

Claim: FACS should be used in classrooms so teachers can read how students feel. Support: a quoted percentage breakdown from D'Alto plus an explanation of the muscle basis (orbicularis oculi, crow's feet); a personal ISAT anecdote with the writer's own emotion percentages and the teacher who could not see them. org 3 (the opening only announces 'I will explain how I think whether' - the position itself does not arrive until the third paragraph, so the controlling idea is stated but weakly located - rung 4 NO); dev 4 (both supports are specific, and the anecdote's connection is stated - 'My teacher couldn't tell my emotions because my emotions was hidden in silence. That's why I feel this technonlogy should be used' - rung 4 YES; the long article-summary paragraph is never connected to the classroom claim, so not most support is explained - rung 5 NO); conv 2 (dense misspelling - caculations, perecnt, txet, strcutered, bsaed - plus 'The answer to that question is rare' and 'I hoep it change the looks at things', where intent has to be guessed rather than repaired - rung 3 NO); arg 4 (the anecdote supplies a genuine why: hidden worry went unnoticed and cost the writer the grade, so a device that surfaces feeling would let teachers act - rung 4 YES; no opposing consideration, no qualification, conclusion is what the prompt implies - rung 5 NO).

Claim: driverless cars have positives and negatives, with positives outweighing. Support: four quotations from 'Driverless Cars Are Coming' (half the fuel of today's taxis; the driver must remain alert; functions up to 25 mph; the in-car system as a safety feature), plus a drunk-driver scenario. org 3 (the opening states only that there are 'both positive and negative aspects'; the actual position - more positives than negatives - appears for the first time in the conclusion, so the controlling idea is weakly located and the body alternates pro, con, pro without building - rung 4 NO); dev 4 (quotations are specific and connections are stated - 'If a person is unable to break fastly the car will do it' - and the alertness quote gets a real addition, but most glosses restate the quotation and the fuel-economy quote is followed by a claim about deaths that does not follow from it - rung 5 NO); conv 3 (benifits, Maufacturers, interpert, 'break fastly', and 'would help that situation a lot less dangerous' need repair; paragraph openers run to one pattern - 'There are a lot of...', 'In paragraph 7 it states' - rung 4 NO); arg 4 (a reason is reasoned - a driver who is drunk or on drugs cannot supply the alertness the system still requires, so not everyone is fit to have one - rung 4 YES; the negatives are reported rather than answered and the conclusion, that negatives will eventually be improved, stays inside the prompt's framing - rung 5 NO).

Claim: driverless cars are a bad idea. Support: delegating driving means teens never learn to drive, with the writer's own drivers-ed case; an undeveloped liability question about who is blamed when the computer wrecks the car. org 4 (position in the first sentence and held, opening and closing both present however thin, both body parts relate - rung 4 YES; the skill-loss and liability parts swap freely - rung 5 NO); dev 3 (the drivers-ed point is the only concrete particular; the liability issue is raised as two questions and abandoned with 'These are some issues that could efect people', and the closing paragraph restates the claim instead of supporting it - the reader supplies the connection - rung 4 NO); conv 2 ('If a computer beggins to start to do the work for us when wont have any work to to do which, sounds beautiful' and 'the dalay teens life' require guessing, not just repair; wreak for wreck and 'are would become' change or break what is said - rung 3 NO); arg 4 (the warrant is on the page: letting a computer drive means never learning to drive, and driving is a large part of a teenager's life, illustrated by the writer refusing a car that would waste what he learned in drivers ed - rung 4 YES; no opposing position engaged, and the close retreats to 'that is just my personal oppion' - rung 5 NO).

Claim: driving bans and car-reduced communities are extreme-sounding but effective. Support: Vauban (parking and garages forbidden, $40,000 for a space, 70 percent car-free, 57 percent sold a car), the EPA's car-reduced push, Paris's alternating plate ban (22-euro fine, almost 4,000 fined, 27 impounded, congestion down 60 percent), and Bogota's car-free days. org 4 (position at the end of para 1 and held to the close, frame present, both body parts relate - rung 4 YES; discounting the 'even harsher' signal the two example sets are parallel lists of the same kind, and Bogota appears in both, so they swap without loss - rung 5 NO); dev 3 (support is abundant and specific but patchwritten - the statistics, the parking prohibitions and the Plaza quotation are lifted with little transformation and sit as source report rather than inside the writer's argument, which caps the trait; results are listed and the reader draws the effectiveness inference); conv 3 (Studdies, Extream, varry, desided, tavis, partisipate, countried accumulate, 'car deduced communities' and 'do to smog' need re-reading to repair, but meaning stays recoverable - rung 4 NO); arg 4 (one reason is reasoned - making parking and garages unavailable and pricing a space at $40,000 is why 70 percent gave up cars - and 'Sounds Extream, but it is very effective' turns a likely objection - rung 4 YES; but the objection is never actually answered and the conclusion is exactly what the prompt's framing implies - rung 5 NO).

Claim: the Electoral College should be replaced by the popular vote because it is unfair and risks disaster. Support: voters actually choose electors who may vote for anyone; a president can lose despite the popular vote; a tie would 'deny the will of the people'. org 3 (controlling idea in the first sentence, but the second paragraph repeats the first without adding to it, and the frame is perfunctory - the essay opens mid-argument and the close is a single re-assertion - rung 4 NO); dev 2 (nothing specific anywhere: no election, no figure, no case, no named source; the elector-defection point is offered three times in different words, and 'it could have disasterous results' restates the claim it is meant to support - rung 3 NO); conv 3 (thew, wouln't, eletoral, disasterous, 'their is', and long coordinated run-ons of one shape - 'if we vote who we want to then we will just get the votes of some electoral voter and if we vote for them they could vote for whoever they wanted to vote for' - force re-reading, but meaning is recoverable - rung 4 NO); arg 3 (position clear and committed throughout - rung 3 YES - but no reason is reasoned: unfairness and the disaster factor are asserted and then circled, each later sentence restating the opening in new words - rung 4 NO).
